subUnits.title: 4.1 Definition, Characteristics, and Types of Prose
notes: Definition, Characteristics, and Types of Prose
Key Concepts:
1. Definition:
- PROSE is literary writing in its ordinary, natural form — without the rhythmic or metrical structure of poetry.
- It is the genre in which most novels, short stories, and essays are written.
2. Characteristics of Prose:
- Written in SENTENCES and PARAGRAPHS (not verse).
- Uses NARRATIVE — a narrator tells the story.
- Can be FICTIONAL (invented) or NON-FICTIONAL (factual).
- Rich in CHARACTER development, SETTING, and PLOT.
3. Types of Prose:
- NOVEL: a long, extended prose fiction with a complex plot and multiple characters.
- SHORT STORY: a brief prose narrative focusing on one main event or impression.
- NOVELLA: a prose work longer than a short story but shorter than a novel.
- ESSAY: a short non-fictional prose piece examining a topic.
- BIOGRAPHY / AUTOBIOGRAPHY: non-fictional prose about a person's life.
Common Mistakes:
- Do NOT assume all prose is fiction — non-fiction (essays, biographies) is equally prose.
- Do NOT confuse a NOVELLA with a NOVEL — a novella is shorter and more focused.

quiz.q: Prose is distinguished from poetry primarily by:
opts: Its use of characters
Its ordinary, natural form without rhythmic or metrical structure
Being always non-fictional
Using only dialogue
quiz.explanation: Prose is written in natural language without the deliberate rhythmic or metrical pattern characteristic of poetry.

quiz.q: Prose is written in:
opts: Stanzas and verses
Acts and scenes
Sentences and paragraphs
Dialogue only
quiz.explanation: Prose is structured in sentences and paragraphs, as opposed to verse or dramatic scenes.

quiz.q: A NOVEL is best described as:
opts: A short prose narrative focusing on one event
A long prose fiction with complex plot and multiple characters
A non-fictional prose piece about a person's life
A brief essay examining one topic
quiz.explanation: A novel is an extended work of prose fiction with developed characters, plot, and setting.

quiz.q: A SHORT STORY differs from a novel in that it:
opts: Is always non-fictional
Has no characters
Is brief and typically focuses on one main event or impression
Must be written in verse
quiz.explanation: A short story is a compact narrative, typically built around a single event, character, or impression.

quiz.q: A NOVELLA is:
opts: Longer than a novel
Shorter than a short story
Longer than a short story but shorter than a novel
Always a biography
quiz.explanation: A novella sits between a short story and a novel in length and scope.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of non-fictional prose?
opts: A novel
A short story
A novella
An autobiography
quiz.explanation: An autobiography is a non-fictional prose work in which a person writes their own life story.

quiz.q: Prose can be:
opts: Only fictional
Only non-fictional
Either fictional or non-fictional
Only written in verse form
quiz.explanation: Prose encompasses both invented fiction (novels, short stories) and factual non-fiction (essays, biographies).

quiz.q: The primary mode of storytelling in prose is:
opts: Stage directions
Verse and rhyme
Narrative description by a narrator
Mime and gesture
quiz.explanation: Prose tells its story through a narrator, using descriptive language — unlike drama which relies on dialogue and action.

quiz.q: An ESSAY is a prose form that:
opts: Always invents fictional characters
Is a short non-fictional piece examining a topic
Is always longer than a novel
Uses verse and rhyme
quiz.explanation: An essay is a relatively short, non-fictional prose piece focused on exploring or arguing about a particular topic.

quiz.q: It is a mistake to assume all prose is fiction because:
opts: All prose is actually poetry
Non-fiction forms like essays and biographies are equally prose
Fiction is not a type of prose
Prose has no non-fictional forms
quiz.explanation: Prose includes both fictional and non-fictional writing — many important prose works are essays, biographies, and journalism.

subUnits.title: 4.2 Narrative Techniques
notes: Narrative Techniques
Key Concepts:
1. Point of View (Narrative Perspective):
- FIRST PERSON: the narrator is a character within the story — uses 'I'. (e.g., 'I walked into the room.')
- THIRD PERSON OMNISCIENT: a narrator outside the story who knows everything about all characters.
- THIRD PERSON LIMITED: an outside narrator who reveals the thoughts of only one character.
- SECOND PERSON: rare — narrator addresses the reader as 'you'.
2. Other Narrative Techniques:
- STREAM OF CONSCIOUSNESS: capturing the continuous flow of a character's thoughts.
- IN MEDIAS RES: beginning the narrative in the middle of the action.
- UNRELIABLE NARRATOR: a narrator whose account is biased, limited, or deliberately deceptive.
- FRAME NARRATIVE: a story within a story — an outer narrative frames an inner one.
Common Mistakes:
- Do NOT confuse FIRST PERSON (character inside the story using 'I') with THIRD PERSON OMNISCIENT (outside narrator knowing everything).
- Do NOT assume an omniscient narrator always tells the complete truth — an author may use an unreliable omniscient voice.

quiz.q: A FIRST PERSON narrator:
opts: Knows everything about all characters from outside the story
Is a character within the story who uses 'I'
Only describes external events without any 'I'
Is always unreliable
quiz.explanation: A first-person narrator is a character within the story, telling events from their personal viewpoint using 'I'.

quiz.q: A THIRD PERSON OMNISCIENT narrator:
opts: Is a character inside the story
Knows the thoughts of only one character
Exists outside the story and knows everything about all characters
Addresses the reader as 'you'
quiz.explanation: The omniscient narrator stands outside the story and has unlimited access to all characters' thoughts and feelings.

quiz.q: A THIRD PERSON LIMITED narrator differs from an omniscient narrator in that:
opts: It uses 'I' throughout
It reveals the inner thoughts of only one character, not all
It stands inside the story as a character
It addresses the reader directly
quiz.explanation: The limited narrator restricts its access to one character's consciousness, unlike the all-knowing omniscient narrator.

quiz.q: IN MEDIAS RES means:
opts: Ending the narrative with a surprise twist
Beginning the narrative in the middle of the action
Telling the story in chronological order
Using a narrator who is unreliable
quiz.explanation: In medias res (Latin: 'into the middle of things') is the technique of beginning a narrative at a key point already in progress.

quiz.q: STREAM OF CONSCIOUSNESS as a narrative technique involves:
opts: A narrator knowing all characters' thoughts
Capturing the continuous, flowing thoughts of a character's mind
Beginning the story in the middle of the action
An outer story framing an inner story
quiz.explanation: Stream of consciousness represents the unbroken, often fragmented flow of a character's inner thoughts.

quiz.q: An UNRELIABLE NARRATOR is one who:
opts: Always tells the complete, objective truth
Provides a biased, limited, or deceptive account of events
Has access to all characters' thoughts simultaneously
Only narrates external events without any perspective
quiz.explanation: An unreliable narrator's account cannot be taken at face value — they may be mistaken, biased, or dishonest.

quiz.q: A FRAME NARRATIVE is:
opts: A narrative beginning in the middle of the action
A narrative using only the second person
A story within a story — an outer narrative framing an inner one
A narrative with a single omniscient narrator
quiz.explanation: A frame narrative uses an outer story to introduce and contain an inner story — like Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.

quiz.q: Second person narration:
opts: Uses 'I' throughout
Addresses the reader directly as 'you'
Is the most common narrative mode in novels
Is the same as third person limited
quiz.explanation: Second person narration is rare and unusual — it directly addresses the reader with 'you', pulling them into the narrative.

quiz.q: Which narrative technique allows the reader the deepest access to ALL characters' inner thoughts?
opts: First person
Third person limited
Second person
Third person omniscient
quiz.explanation: The omniscient narrator has unrestricted access to the inner worlds of all characters.

quiz.q: It is a mistake to confuse first person with third person omniscient because:
opts: They both use 'I'
A first person narrator is inside the story using 'I'; an omniscient narrator is outside knowing everything
Third person omniscient is always more reliable
First person can also know all characters' thoughts
quiz.explanation: The critical difference is perspective: first person is inside and limited to personal experience; omniscient is outside and all-knowing.

subUnits.title: 4.3 Character Types, and Further Prose Vocabulary
notes: Character Types, and Further Prose Vocabulary
Key Concepts:
1. Character Types:
- PROTAGONIST: the central character whose journey drives the narrative.
- ANTAGONIST: the character or force opposing the protagonist.
- ROUND character: complex, multidimensional — capable of growth and change.
- FLAT character: one-dimensional, defined by a single trait.
- STOCK character: a recognisable type (the miser, the hero's loyal friend).
- FOIL: a character whose contrasting traits highlight the qualities of another character.
2. Further Prose Vocabulary:
- SETTING: the time and place in which the story unfolds.
- THEME: the central idea or message the author explores.
- MOTIF: a recurring image, symbol, or idea throughout the text.
- DICTION: the author's choice of words, contributing to tone and style.
- IMAGERY: vivid, descriptive language that appeals to the senses.
Common Mistakes:
- Do NOT confuse THEME (central idea) with PLOT (sequence of events) — the plot carries the theme, but they are distinct.
- Do NOT confuse FOIL (contrasting character) with ANTAGONIST (opposing force) — a foil may actually be friendly to the protagonist.

quiz.q: A FOIL character is:
opts: The main character of the story
A character whose contrasting traits highlight the qualities of another character
An antagonist who opposes the protagonist
A one-dimensional, stereotypical character
quiz.explanation: A foil character exists to contrast with another — usually the protagonist — making the other's traits more vivid by comparison.

quiz.q: THEME in a prose text refers to:
opts: The sequence of events that make up the story
The time and place in which the story is set
The central idea or message the author explores
The author's choice of words
quiz.explanation: Theme is the underlying idea or message — what the story is really 'about' beyond the surface events.

quiz.q: A MOTIF in a text is:
opts: The setting of the story
A recurring image, symbol, or idea that reinforces the theme
The main character's fatal flaw
The climax of the plot
quiz.explanation: A motif is a recurring element — an image, object, or idea — that appears throughout a text with thematic significance.

quiz.q: DICTION refers to:
opts: The plot structure of a novel
The author's deliberate choice of words, contributing to tone and style
The setting of the story
The climax of the narrative
quiz.explanation: Diction is the specific word choices an author makes — formal or informal, simple or complex — which shape the tone and voice of the text.

quiz.q: IMAGERY in prose uses language that:
opts: Only tells the reader facts without description
Appeals to the senses to create vivid mental pictures
Avoids any descriptive language
Only addresses the reader directly
quiz.explanation: Imagery uses descriptive, sensory language to help the reader vividly experience the scenes and emotions of the narrative.

quiz.q: SETTING encompasses:
opts: Only the physical location of the story
The central idea the author explores
The time AND place in which the story unfolds
The sequence of major events
quiz.explanation: Setting includes both the geographic location and the historical/temporal context of the narrative.

quiz.q: A ROUND character is distinguished by:
opts: Being one-dimensional and defined by a single trait
Being a recognisable type or stereotype
Being complex, multidimensional, and capable of change
Always opposing the protagonist
quiz.explanation: Round characters are fully developed and lifelike — they can surprise the reader and change throughout the story.

quiz.q: Theme differs from plot in that:
opts: Plot is the idea; theme is the events
Theme is the central idea; plot is the sequence of events carrying that idea
They are the same thing
Only novels have themes; only dramas have plots
quiz.explanation: The plot is what happens; the theme is what it means. The plot is the vehicle for the theme.

quiz.q: A STOCK character is:
opts: The most complex character in the story
A character whose contrasting traits highlight another's qualities
A recognisable type with familiar traits (e.g., the miser, the loyal sidekick)
Always the protagonist
quiz.explanation: Stock characters are recognisable archetypes drawn from established conventions — readers immediately understand their role.

quiz.q: A foil is NOT the same as an antagonist because:
opts: A foil always kills the protagonist
A foil may be friendly to the protagonist and exists to create contrast, not necessarily conflict
An antagonist contrasts with the protagonist; a foil opposes them
They are exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: A foil creates contrast to illuminate another character's traits — this role can be filled by a friend, not just an opponent.
